inline.s: The path of practice in the Platform Sutra is “to know your own original mind, and to see your own original nature.” The point at which one sets to work is the contemplation of the mind—turning the light back upon one’s own mind. Thus the Sixth Patriarch, in an earnest and weighty tone, exhorted: each of you should gaze into your own mind and see your own nature.
The method of turning the light back upon one’s own mind is this:
When a thought arises, know it and do not follow it; when a thought subsides, be still and yet clearly aware.

To contemplate and thereby attain samadhi—this is the samadhi of true reality (tathata), king of samadhis, and is therefore called the supreme samadhi. The Treatise on the Awakening of the Bodhi Mind says: “When a deluded thought arises (i.e. when a thought rises), know it and do not follow it; when the delusion subsides (i.e. when the thought is stilled), the mind-source is empty and still, all virtues are complete, and its wondrous functions are inexhaustible.”

[Know it and do not follow it] Gaze upon the thought without adding judgments. The key to “know it and do not follow it” lies in doing the work upon “knowing”—watching as a cat keeps watch over a mouse’s hole: the moment a thought rises, you know it. Once “knowing the instant a thought rises” is achieved, “not following” becomes easy. [Stillness with bright awareness] This is no-thought, clearly knowing that it is no-thought. The Treatise on Cutting Off Delusion says: “The still, calm extinction of the mind-nature is samadhi; the constant understanding of that extinction is prajna.” This is to say: when the mind-nature abides in the state of still extinction, this is called samadhi; and when one knows clearly and unceasingly that at this moment the mind-nature is in that state of extinction, this is called prajna. Thus, stillness with bright awareness is the even upholding of samadhi and prajna. [Mind-source] The mind is the source of the myriad dharmas, and so it is called the mind-source. [All virtues complete] All virtues are then complete. “Then” (si) means “then, thereby.” Example sentence: With preparedness, one then has no calamity.

The Treatise on Destroying Delusion says: “The single dharma of contemplating the mind gathers up all dharmas and is the most essential and concise.” The Nirvana Sutra says: “To be able to contemplate the mind-nature is called the supreme samadhi.”

The Fourth Patriarch Daoxin said: “All the hundred and thousand Dharma-gates alike return to this single square inch; the boundless, river-sand-like wondrous virtues all rest in the mind-source. All the gates of precepts, of samadhi, and of wisdom, together with the powers of spiritual transformation, are all inherently complete, and do not depart from your mind.”
Therefore the root of the Buddha-Dharma lies in the mind, and the root of practice lies in contemplation.
To turn the light back upon oneself constantly—this is prajna fumigating ignorance. The moment ignorance is broken, the dharmakaya manifests at once.

In a single leap one enters directly the ground of the Tathagata, and without passing through asankhya kalpas one attains the dharmakaya. The Perfect Enlightenment Sutra says: “All Tathagatas, from the causal ground in which they first arose, all rely on the perfect illumination of the pure, clear knowing-nature, and only by eternally cutting off ignorance do they accomplish the Buddha-way.”

The core of practice after awakening is to remove habitual tendencies in order to cut off afflictions; and contemplation of the mind is the keen instrument for removing those habits. So one must use the contemplation of the mind to remove habits and to do the “three no’s” work (see the section “The Three No’s Work” in “Chapter Four, Samadhi and Prajna”).

[If you cannot awaken by yourself, you must seek out a great good-knowing friend (kalyanamitra), one who understands the supreme Dharma-vehicle, so that he may directly point out the right path. This good-knowing friend bears a great karmic connection, being one whose teaching and guidance cause you to see your nature. All good dharmas are set in motion because the good-knowing friend can arouse them. The twelve sections of the scriptures of the Buddhas of the three times are inherently complete within the nature of beings. If you cannot awaken by yourself, you must seek the pointing of a good-knowing friend to see; if you can awaken by yourself, then you need no seeking outside.]

If one cannot awaken by oneself, one must seek out an illuminating teacher (the great good-knowing friend who understands the supreme Dharma-vehicle) to directly point out the right path. Because of a great karmic connection with him from past lives, his teaching and guidance can cause one to see one’s nature. All the wondrous dharmas that guide practice toward realization are set in motion precisely because the good-knowing friend can arouse them. The twelve sections of the scriptures of the Buddhas of the three times are inherently complete within the nature of sentient beings. Yet one who cannot awaken by himself must seek the instruction of a good-knowing friend to see his nature; if one can awaken by oneself, then no seeking outside is needed.

[If one obstinately clings to the notion that one must rely upon a good-knowing friend, and from him expects to gain liberation, there is no such principle. Why? Because within one’s own mind there is a good-knowing friend able to cause self-awakening. If one gives rise to deviant confusion and inverted, delusive thoughts, then even though a good-knowing friend without should teach, one cannot be saved. If one raises the true and correct contemplation of prajna, in a single instant all delusive thoughts are extinguished; if one recognizes one’s own nature, in one awakening one reaches the ground of Buddhahood.]

If one obstinately insists that one must rely upon a good-knowing friend, hoping through him to gain liberation, there is no such principle. Why? Because within one’s own mind there is a good-knowing friend able to guide one to awakening. If one gives rise to deviant confusion and inverted, delusive thoughts, then even though a good-knowing friend without should teach, one still cannot be saved; if one raises the true prajna contemplation, in a single instant all delusive thoughts vanish and one can awaken; if one recognizes one’s own original nature, in one awakening one reaches the ground of Buddhahood.

arising in deviant confusion” and “arising in the true contemplation of prajna” have utterly different results; therefore the practitioner must at all times and everywhere be alert to whether he is “arising in deviant confusion” or “arising in the true contemplation of prajna.”

[Within one’s own mind there is a good-knowing friend] Within one’s own mind there is a good-knowing friend—what is commonly called the “inner teacher.” To rouse one’s own “inner teacher” is truly a most vital matter.
Q. How does one rouse one’s own “inner teacher”?
A. “Still your thoughts and forget your deliberations, and the Buddha appears before you of itself.” (Essentials of Mind Transmission)

[Good-knowing friends! Contemplate with prajna wisdom, so that within and without are clearly illumined, and you know your own original mind. If you know your original mind, you are fundamentally liberated. If you attain liberation, that is the samadhi of prajna, that is “no-thought.”]

Good-knowing friends! Contemplate with prajna wisdom (that is, the “true contemplation of prajna” spoken of above), so that within and without are clearly illumined, and you know your own original mind. If you know your own original mind, you attain the fundamental liberation. If you attain the fundamental liberation, that is the samadhi of prajna, that is no-thought.

[Know your own original mind] This is to realize within oneself the mind’s original state—luminous, clear, and deeply still. The Mahayana Sutra of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground says: “If one can contemplate that the nature and essence of the mind is empty, then the delusions and obstructions do not arise, and one is liberated.” [Fundamental liberation] The mind being empty, the realms are empty of themselves; the myriad dharmas bind nothing, and are fundamentally liberated.

[What is called no-thought? If, upon seeing all dharmas, the mind does not become defiled by grasping, this is no-thought. In its functioning it reaches everywhere, yet it does not grasp at any place. Only purify your original mind, causing the six consciousnesses to issue out through the six gates, and amid the six dusts to be without defilement and without mixture, coming and going freely, functioning universally without obstruction—this is the samadhi of prajna, ease and liberation, called the practice of no-thought. If one ceases to think of the hundred things and causes thought to be utterly cut off, that is bondage to dharmas, and is called a biased view.]

What is called “no-thought”? If, upon seeing the myriad things (all dharmas), the mind does not become defiled by grasping (that is, does not discriminate and reckon, does not indulge in delusive imaginings and clinging, is without love and hate, liking and disliking), this is no-thought. The mind, in functioning, reaches everywhere, yet does not grasp at any place. Only purify your original mind, causing the six consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, and mind-consciousness) to issue out through the six gates (that is, the six sense-organs: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind), and amid the six dusts
(form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and dharma)

—neither mingled with greed, hatred, and delusion, nor defiled by greed, hatred, and delusion—coming and going freely, functioning universally without obstruction, this is the samadhi of prajna, ease and liberation, called the “practice of no-thought.” If one thinks of nothing whatsoever and suppresses thought so that it does not arise, that is bondage to dharmas, and is called a biased view.

Therefore “no-thought” is not to be without thoughts at all; rather it is: upon seeing all dharmas, the mind does not cling, has no delusive imaginings or clinging, no love and hate, no liking and disliking. As the Diamond Sutra says: “Think not with a mind dwelling on form, think not with a mind dwelling on sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma; think with a mind that dwells nowhere.” That is to say: merely keep one’s own thought free from the realms, and do not let the mind be born upon a dharma.

[Cause thought to be utterly cut off] Not permitting thought to arise. [Bondage to dharmas] A one-sided clinging to dharmas, taking passages out of context and not knowing how to apply them flexibly—so that one is fettered by them and cannot be liberated. [Biased view] An evil view that leans to one side (rushing off to an opposite extreme).
This sutra says:
“If one ceases to think of the hundred things and causes thought to be utterly cut off, that is bondage to dharmas, and is called a biased view.”

Therefore correct practice is not to cease thinking of the hundred things, but rather to awaken at the place of seeing, hearing, and knowing. The “seeing, hearing, and knowing” that arises when the six sense-organs contact the six dusts, though the root of delusive thought, is also the essential gate for awakening and entering the Way. The difference between “delusion” and “awakening” lies solely in whether, at the place of seeing, hearing, and knowing, one can turn delusion into awakening and consciousness into wisdom. As a later passage says:
“The true-suchness self-nature gives rise to thought; though the six sense-organs have seeing, hearing, and knowing, they are not defiled by the myriad realms.”

[Awakening] To see all dharmas with a mind that does not become defiled by grasping (that does not discriminate and reckon, does not indulge in delusive imaginings and clinging, is without love and hate, liking and disliking).

[Good-knowing friends! One who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought penetrates all the myriad dharmas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought sees the realms of all the Buddhas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought reaches the stage of Buddhahood.]

Good-knowing friends! One who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought reaches through all the Buddha-Dharmas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought sees the realms of all the Buddhas; one who awakens to the Dharma of no-thought reaches the stage of Buddhahood.
How I praise the Dharma of no-thought!

[Good-knowing friends! Those in later ages who gain my Dharma, let them, toward those of like view and like practice, vow to receive and hold this Sudden-Teaching Dharma-gate. Because in so doing they serve the Buddha, those who to the end of life never retreat will surely enter the stage of the sages. Yet one must transmit the silent transmission and charge handed down from the patriarchs of old, and must not conceal the true Dharma. If they are of unlike view and unlike practice, dwelling in another Dharma, one must not transmit and entrust it to them; for that would injure the common-goods of those former worthies, and in the end be of no benefit. I fear that foolish people, not understanding, will slander this Dharma-gate, and for a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives cut off the seed of Buddhahood.]

Good-knowing friends! Those in later ages who gain my Dharma should, together with those of like view and like practice, vow to receive and hold this Sudden-Teaching Dharma-gate. Because receiving and holding the Sudden Teaching is like serving the Buddha, those who persist to the end of life without retreat will surely enter the stage of the sages. But to them (those of like view and like practice) one must transmit the silent transmission and charge handed down through all the successive patriarchs, and must not conceal the true Dharma of the Sudden Teaching. If they are of unlike view, unlike practice, and dwell in other Dharma-gates, one must not transmit and entrust it to them; because this would injure the reputations of their former ancestors and masters, and in the end be harmful and profitless both to them and to oneself. In particular, I fear that foolish people, not understanding the Sudden Teaching, will slander this Dharma-gate and incur the grave retribution, over a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives, of cutting off the seed of Buddhahood.

“No-marks” means not clinging to marks (not grasping characteristics as real). Why must one not cling to marks? Because “all marks whatsoever are false.” From beginningless kalpas, we, precisely because we clung to marks, were enticed, coerced, and bound by marks, and so created karma and received retribution—hence there is birth and death, and the wheel of transmigration. Now, in order to end birth and death and escape the three realms, we must depart from marks and no longer cling to them. The Verse of No-Marks tells us how not to cling to marks. If one can recite it again and again, realize it again and again, practice it again and again, and test it again and again, the results will surely be great.

[Good-knowing friends! I have a Verse of No-Marks; each of you must recite and take it up. Both lay and monastic, simply practice according to it. If you do not practice it, but only bear in mind my words, it will likewise be of no benefit. Listen to my verse:]

Good-knowing friends! I have a Verse of No-Marks; each of you must recite, receive, and hold it. Both lay and monastic, simply practice according to it; if you do not actually practice it yourself, but only bear in mind my words, there is also no benefit. Listen to my verse:
[Through speech and through the mind, as the sun that dwells in the empty sky, so to transmit the Dharma of seeing nature, I have come forth from the world to destroy the false sects.]

Through speech and through the mind—like a radiant sun at the zenith illuminating the whole world. To transmit the Sudden-Teaching Dharma of seeing one’s nature and becoming Buddha, I have come into this world to destroy the false sects.

[Through speech (shuo-tong)] One who is well versed in the scriptures and, responding to the capacities of sentient beings, speaks the Dharma with skillfully appropriate means, is called one who is through in speech; one who can awaken to the essential purpose, knowing his own original mind and seeing his own original nature, is called one who is through in the essential. The Lankavatara Sutra says: “All sravakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas have two kinds of throughness—the throughness of the essential and the throughness of speech.” [Through the essential] This is the throughness of the essential (zong-tong). [False sects] The Chan school calls all sects that do not take seeing one’s nature as their essential aim “false sects.” Why? Because these sects hold that there is Dharma outside the mind, and so they cling to marks. For this reason the verse is named “No-Marks.” [No-marks] Amid all marks, to be free of all marks.
[The Dharma has neither sudden nor gradual, but confusion and awakening are slow or quick. Only this gate of seeing one’s nature—the foolish cannot fully know it.]

The Dharma originally has neither sudden nor gradual; rather, sentient beings’ confusion and awakening are slow or quick. But this Dharma-gate of seeing one’s nature is something that foolish and deluded people cannot comprehend.
[Speaking is of a myriad kinds, yet being in accord with principle it returns to one. In the dark dwelling of affliction, ever must be born the sun of wisdom.]

Though the teachings are many and varied, their principle is one: in the dark dwelling of affliction, one must at all times contemplate with the principle of prajna (let the sun of wisdom be born). (This is what was said above: “Contemplate with prajna wisdom, so that within and without are clearly illumined, and you know your own original mind.”)

[In the dark dwelling of affliction, ever must be born the sun of wisdom] By contemplating with the principle of prajna (the contemplation of wisdom), deviant thoughts naturally cannot stain it, just as when the sun is in the sky the mountain-sprites sink away unnoticed.
[When the deviant comes, afflictions arrive; when the right comes, afflictions are removed. When deviant and right are both put aside, purity is reached with nothing left over.]
When a deviant thought arises, afflictions arrive; when a right thought arises, afflictions are removed; when neither a deviant nor a right thought is used, then one reaches complete purity.
[Bodhi is intrinsically self-nature; to stir the mind is to be false. To purify the mind amid the false—only uprightness, and the three hindrances are gone.]

Bodhi is the awareness inherently complete in self-nature; to stir the mind gives rise to illusions. To purify the mind amid illusion, one need only maintain right thought, and then there are no three hindrances (the hindrance of afflictions, the hindrance of karma, and the hindrance of retribution).

[The three hindrances] There are three that veil the right Way: the hindrance of afflictions, the hindrance of karma, and the hindrance of retribution. The hindrance of afflictions is the obstacle caused by the delusions of greed, hatred, and ignorance; the hindrance of karma is the obstacle caused by karmic actions; the hindrance of retribution is the obstacle caused by the fruits of retribution.
[If people of the world would cultivate the Way, nothing whatever obstructs them. Ever seeing one’s own faults—this is to be in accord with the Way.]
If people of the world cultivate the Way, nothing at all obstructs them; ever aware of one’s own faults, one is in accord with the Way.
[Ever see one’s own faults] Here “fault” does not mean a mistake in one’s doing, but rather becoming defiled by the dust-realms and following the emotions to create karma.

Regarding the faults of one’s own mind, the Great Master Hanshan said: “Those who in ancient times studied the Way, the very first thing was that the mind concerning birth and death must be earnest—not that they sought some profound and mysterious principle. What is this ‘birth and death’? It is precisely our common, present-day experience: amid the many states of worldly dust and toil, when one meets a circumstance or encounters a condition, whether adverse or favorable, the inner habitual tendencies call forth manifested activity, giving rise to such discriminating, delusive minds as love and hate, grasping and rejecting, and so forth. Because thought after thought clings and attaches, and gives rise to karma of many kinds, good and evil, all of these become the very root of future birth and death. Since delusive thought is boundless, so birth and death is without end. Hence sentient beings, through long kalpas revolving in the bitter sea of birth and death, have no moment of getting out—this is wholly because they do not know the faults of their own mind.” (Dream Journey Collection
[Beings possessed of color each have their own Way, and should none hinder or trouble the other. To leave the Way and seek another way—to the end of life one never sees the Way.]
